claim: The eukaryotic genome exists in the form of chromatin, with the basic repeating nucleosome subunit a core-histone octamer (two each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4) wrapped by ~147 base pairs of DNA.
source: The eukaryotic genome exists in the form of chromatin, with the basic repeating nucleosome subunit a core-histone octamer (two each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4) wrapped by ~147 base pairs of DNA (Figure 1a; Luger et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Luger et al., 1997, which is a foundational structural study of the nucleosome.

claim: Particular histone PTMs are correlated with distinct chromatin states (e.g. transcriptional activation/repression, damaged DNA) and/or genomic elements (e.g. gene promoters, transcriptional enhancers, centromeres).
source: Globally speaking, particular histone PTMs are correlated with distinct chromatin states (e.g. transcriptional activation/repression, damaged DNA) and/or genomic elements (e.g. gene promoters, transcriptional enhancers, centromeres) (Wang et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2011; Rivera and Ren, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Wang et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2011; Rivera and Ren, 2013) that document correlations between histone PTMs and chromatin states.

claim: It has been proposed that histone PTMs function in diverse combinations, perhaps even forming a 'histone code'.
source: Importantly, it has been proposed that the PTMs function in diverse combinations, perhaps even forming a 'histone code' (Strahl and Allis, 2000; Gardner et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2010) read by chromatin associated proteins (CAPs) via their various 'reader domains,' thus localizing and/or regulating CAP activity (Rothbart and Strahl, 2014; Andrews et al., 2016a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational papers on the histone code hypothesis (Strahl and Allis, 2000; Gardner et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2010) and reader domain function (Rothbart and Strahl, 2014; Andrews et al., 2016a).

claim: The BPTF subunit is important for chromatin association of the NURF (Nucleosome Remodeling Factor) complex.
source: The BPTF subunit is important for chromatin association of the NURF (Nucleosome Remodeling Factor) complex (Wysocka et al., 2006; Li et al., 2006), and pro-tumorigenic in several malignancies (Zahid et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating BPTF's role in NURF complex chromatin association (Wysocka et al., 2006; Li et al., 2006).

claim: BPTF is pro-tumorigenic in several malignancies.
source: The BPTF subunit is important for chromatin association of the NURF (Nucleosome Remodeling Factor) complex (Wysocka et al., 2006; Li et al., 2006), and pro-tumorigenic in several malignancies (Zahid et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zahid et al., 2021b documenting BPTF's role in cancer.

claim: The BPTF PHD finger associates with H3 tri-methylated at lysine 4 (H3K4me3) in the context of histone peptides.
source: In the context of histone peptides, the PHD associates with H3 tri-methylated at lysine 4 (H3K4me3) (Li et al., 2006), while the BD binds H3 and H4 tails containing acetylated lysines (Kac), with a preference for H4 (Ruthenburg et al., 2011; Li et al., 2006; Olson et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2006 demonstrating PHD binding to H3K4me3 peptides.

claim: The BPTF bromodomain binds H3 and H4 tails containing acetylated lysines, with a preference for H4 in peptide context.
source: In the context of histone peptides, the PHD associates with H3 tri-methylated at lysine 4 (H3K4me3) (Li et al., 2006), while the BD binds H3 and H4 tails containing acetylated lysines (Kac), with a preference for H4 (Ruthenburg et al., 2011; Li et al., 2006; Olson et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing bromodomain binding preferences (Ruthenburg et al., 2011; Li et al., 2006; Olson et al., 2020).

claim: Previous studies suggested BPTF PHD-BD prefers [H3K4me3, H4tetraac] or [H3K4me3, H4K16ac] on nucleosomes.
source: While efforts have been made to investigate the recruitment of BPTF PHD-BD to modified nucleosomes, only a limited subset of H3K4me3/H4Kac combinations based on peptide data have been tested, suggesting a preference for [H3K4me3, H4K5acK8acK12acK16ac (hereafter H4tetraac)] (Ruthenburg et al., 2011) or [H3K4me3, H4K16ac] (Ruthenburg et al., 2011; Nguyen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Ruthenburg et al., 2011; Nguyen et al., 2014) that tested limited nucleosome combinations.

claim: GST-PHD-BD showed strong selectivity for methylated H3K4 peptides over all other methyl-residues represented (me1-2-3 at H3K9, H3K27, H3K36, and H4K20).
source: In agreement with previous studies (Wysocka et al., 2006; Li et al., 2006), the GST-PHD-BD Query showed strong selectivity for methylated H3K4 peptides over all other methyl-residues represented (me1-2-3 at H3K9, H3K27, H3K36, and H4K20: Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b and is consistent with prior citations (Wysocka et al., 2006; Li et al., 2006).

claim: GST-PHD-BD preferred acetylated H4 tail peptides with little difference in binding to multiply acetylated tail vs. any singly acetylated residue.
source: Also in agreement with previously (Ruthenburg et al., 2011; Nguyen et al., 2014), GST-PHD-BD preferred acetylated H4 tail peptides, though we observed little difference in binding to a multiply acetylated tail vs. any singly acetylated residue on the same (Figure 1c and e and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1c, e, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b, and is consistent with prior studies (Ruthenburg et al., 2011; Nguyen et al., 2014).

claim: GST-PHD-BD showed comparable binding to singly or multiply acetylated H3 tail peptides, though with approximately twofold weaker EC50rel compared to H4 peptides.
source: We also observed comparable binding to singly or multiply acetylated H3 tail peptides, though with approximately twofold weaker EC50rel as compared to H4 peptides (Figure 1c and e and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c, e, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: GST-PHD-BD showed no preference for H3K4me3K9acK14acK18ac peptide over peptides containing each PTM class alone.
source: Finally, and again in agreement with previously (Chen et al., 2020), we observed no preference for a H3K4me3K9acK14acK18ac (hereafter H3K4me3triac) peptide over those containing each PTM class alone (Figure 1c and e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1c and e, and is consistent with Chen et al., 2020.

claim: The overall affinity of GST-PHD-BD for nucleosomes was reduced relative to peptides.
source: We next examined the interaction of GST-PHD-BD with PTM-defined NCPs and found several striking differences. First, the overall affinity for nucleosomes was reduced relative to peptides (Figure 1c–e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing peptide and nucleosome binding shown in Figure 1c-e.

claim: NCPs recapitulated only a subset of the interactions observed with peptides for GST-PHD-BD.
source: Second, NCPs recapitulated only a subset of the interactions observed with peptides (Figure 1c–e and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing peptide and nucleosome binding patterns shown in multiple figures.

claim: GST-PHD-BD showed newfound selectivity for H3K4me3 over the me2/me1 states in nucleosomes.
source: Differences included a newfound selectivity for H3K4me3 over the me2 /me1 states (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d and e), and binding to acetylated H3 but not acetylated H4 (Figure 1d and e and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d and e.

claim: GST-PHD-BD bound to acetylated H3 but not acetylated H4 in nucleosomes.
source: Differences included a newfound selectivity for H3K4me3 over the me2 /me1 states (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d and e), and binding to acetylated H3 but not acetylated H4 (Figure 1d and e and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d, e, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b and c.

claim: GST-PHD-BD showed a dramatic increase in affinity for NCPs containing H3K4me3triac combinatorial vs. those containing each PTM class alone (26-fold over H3K4me3; 20-fold over H3tetraac).
source: A third contrast to peptides was a dramatic increase in the affinity of GST-PHD-BD for NCPs containing the H3K4me3triac combinatorial vs. those containing each PTM class alone (26-fold over H3K4me3; 20-fold over H3K4acK9acK14acK18ac (hereafter H3tetraac)) (Figure 1d and e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing fold-change differences in EC50rel values presented in Figure 1d and e.

claim: GST-PHD-BD showed similar EC50rel to H3K4me3triac for H3K4me3K14ac and H3K4me3K18ac, but fourfold weaker for H3K4me3K9ac.
source: We observed a similar EC50rel to H3K4me3triac for H3K4me3K14ac and H3K4me3K18ac, but fourfold weaker for H3K4me3K9ac (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f and g).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing EC50rel values shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1f and g.

claim: Crystal structures of BPTF BD in complex with acetylated histone peptides indicate the bromodomain binding pocket can accommodate only one acetyl-lysine.
source: Notably, crystal structures of BPTF BD in complex with acetylated histone peptides (Ruthenburg et al., 2011) indicate the bromodomain binding pocket can accommodate only one acetyl-lysine.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to structural studies (Ruthenburg et al., 2011).

claim: BPTF PHD-BD preferentially reads out nucleosomal H3K4me3K14ac or H3K4me3K18ac.
source: Thus, data supports that PHD-BD preferentially reads out nucleosomal H3K4me3K14ac or H3K4me3K18ac.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing differential binding to individual acetylated forms.

claim: The 6His-PHD affinity for NCPs was reduced relative to peptides.
source: As for the PHD-BD tandem, the 6His-PHD affinity for NCPs was reduced relative to peptides (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–d and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a-d and Supplementary file 1.

claim: 6His-PHD preferentially associated with H3K4me3 and approximately twofold weaker to H3K4me3triac peptides, but this order was inverted for NCPs.
source: Interestingly, while 6His-PHD was preferentially associated with H3K4me3 and approximately twofold weaker to H3K4me3triac peptides, this order was inverted for NCPs (compare Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and c and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing peptide and nucleosome binding shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a-d.

claim: GST-PHD favored NCPs with H3K4me3 and co-incident acetyl-lysine, but had no preference between K9ac, K14ac, or K18ac.
source: The same affinity trends were observed for GST-PHD, which favored NCPs with H3K4me3 and co-incident acetyl-lysine, but had no preference between K9ac, K14ac, or K18ac (see 'Materials and methods' and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and e.

claim: 6His-BD bound both acetylated H3 and H4 peptides, but with a preference for acetylated H4.
source: Regarding the bromodomain, 6His-BD bound both acetylated H3 and H4 peptides, but with a preference for acetylated H4 (Ruthenburg et al., 2011; Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and f, and is consistent with Ruthenburg et al., 2011.

claim: 6His-BD failed to bind any tested nucleosome targets.
source: However, when presented with NCPs, it failed to bind any tested targets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and g).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and g.

claim: GST-PHDmut-BD lost binding to all tested nucleosome targets (including H3K4me3, H3tetraac, or H3K4me3triac).
source: On NCPs, GST-PHDmut-BD lost binding to all tested targets (including H3K4me3, H3tetraac, or H3K4me3triac), while GST-PHD-BDmut bound H3K4me3 weaker than H3K4me3triac but did not associate with H3tetraac (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutant studies shown in Figure 2b and c.

claim: GST-PHD-BDmut bound H3K4me3 weaker than H3K4me3triac but did not associate with H3tetraac.
source: On NCPs, GST-PHDmut-BD lost binding to all tested targets (including H3K4me3, H3tetraac, or H3K4me3triac), while GST-PHD-BDmut bound H3K4me3 weaker than H3K4me3triac but did not associate with H3tetraac (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutant studies shown in Figure 2b and c.

claim: A functional BD is insufficient to mediate NCP binding without a functional PHD in the tandem context.
source: This revealed that even in the tandem context a functional BD is insufficient to mediate NCP binding without a functional PHD.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the mutant studies showing that PHD mutation abolishes binding even when BD is functional.

claim: Chemical shift perturbations in BD resonances were observed on addition of H3triac, H3tetraac, or H3K4me3triac peptides to 15N-labeled PHD-BD.
source: To investigate this, we used NMR spectroscopy to record sequential 1H,15N-HSQC spectra on 15N-labeled PHD-BD after addition of unlabeled H3triac, H3tetraac, or H3K4me3triac peptides (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–c). Chemical shift perturbations (CSPs) in BD resonances were observed on addition of all three peptides, indicating ligand engagement.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-c.

claim: The bound state chemical shift of BD was similar for H3triac, H3tetraac, and H3K4me3triac peptides, suggesting an association mechanism independent of H3K4 modification state.
source: Further, the bound state chemical shift was similar for all three peptides, suggesting an association mechanism independent of H3K4 modification state (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is inferred from NMR data showing similar chemical shifts across different peptides in Figure 3a.

claim: For PHD resonances, the H3K4 modification state elicited distinct CSPs, with H3tetraac and H3triac showing nearly identical bound state chemical shifts vs. that for H3K4me3triac.
source: However, for PHD resonances the H3K4 modification state elicited distinct CSPs, with H3tetraac and H3triac showing nearly identical bound state chemical shifts vs. that for H3K4me3triac (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data showing differential chemical shifts for PHD resonances in Figure 3a.

claim: PHD-BD associates with the acetylated H3 tail likely in a multivalent manner, employing both domains independent of H3K4 modification status, but forming a unique complex when H3K4 is trimethylated.
source: Together this reveals that PHD-BD associates with the acetylated H3 tail likely in a multivalent manner, employing both domains independent of H3K4 modification status, but forming a unique complex when H3K4 is trimethylated.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the NMR data showing differential binding modes depending on H3K4 methylation state.

claim: Histone H3-A1 is essential for 6His-PHD-BD binding to NCPs.
source: To test this, we truncated A1 in the context of H3K4me3triac and observed PHD-BD was unable to bind the resulting NCP (NΔ1) (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing loss of binding upon A1 truncation in Figure 3b.

claim: Recognition of the H3 N-terminus is critical for BPTF PHD engagement, consistent with the binding mechanism for other PHD fingers.
source: Thus, recognition of the H3 N-terminus is critical for BPTF PHD engagement, an observation consistent with the binding mechanism for other PHD fingers (Musselman et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on A1 truncation and is consistent with prior studies on PHD fingers (Musselman et al., 2009).

claim: The H4 tail is K/R-rich, has decreased dynamics in the nucleosome vs. peptide context.
source: The H4 tail is K/R-rich, has decreased dynamics in the nucleosome vs. peptide context, and computational models suggest it may also form a fuzzy complex with DNA (Rabdano et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rabdano et al., 2021 which includes computational modeling.

claim: Only 15 of the 101 non-proline amino-acids of H4 were observable by NMR in the nucleosome context, corresponding to tail residues 1–15.
source: Consistent with previously (Rabdano et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2023) we observed resonances for only 15 of the 101 non-proline amino-acids of H4, corresponding to tail residues 1–15 (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 4 and is consistent with prior studies (Rabdano et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2023).

claim: The severe line-broadening observed for H4 residues 16–20 (the H4 tail basic patch) indicates this region is likely stably associated with the nucleosome core.
source: The severe line-broadening observed for residues 16–20 (the H4 tail basic patch: Figure 4—figure supplement 2) indicates this region is likely stably associated with the nucleosome core, in agreement with previous structural and biochemical studies (Zheng and Hayes, 2003)
evidence: This claim is inferred from NMR line-broadening data and is consistent with prior structural studies (Zheng and Hayes, 2003).

claim: Overlay of 15N-H4 peptide and 15N-H4-NCP NMR spectra showed chemical shift perturbations in every H4 tail resonance when comparing peptide and NCP.
source: Overlay of the resulting NMR spectra showed CSPs in every H4 tail resonance when comparing peptide and NCP (Figure 4a), consistent with a context-dependent conformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The 15N-H4 (1-25) peptide showed CSPs for every resonance upon addition of unlabeled DNA, confirming the H4 tail bound DNA.
source: We next collected sequential 1H,15N-HSQC spectra of the 15N-H4 (1-25) peptide upon addition of unlabeled DNA (Figure 4b), and observed CSPs for every resonance, confirming the H4 tail bound DNA, and every residue is impacted.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR titration data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Overlay of the DNA-bound 15N-H4 peptide and 15N-H4-NCP spectra showed very similar chemical shifts, consistent with the entire H4 tail associating with nucleosomal DNA.
source: Overlay of the DNA-bound 15N-H4 peptide and 15N-H4-NCP spectra showed very similar chemical shifts, consistent with the entire H4 tail associating with nucleosomal DNA (Figure 4c), and in-line with previous cross-linking and molecular dynamics simulation studies (Murphy et al., 2017; Karch et al., 2018; Mullahoo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data in Figure 4c and is consistent with prior cross-linking and simulation studies (Murphy et al., 2017; Karch et al., 2018; Mullahoo et al., 2020).

claim: The H4 tail has two distinct dynamic regions: residues 1–15 likely exchange quickly between multiple conformations on DNA, while residues 16–20 exchange much more slowly and/or between fewer states.
source: The differential linewidth of resonances indicates the H4 tail has two distinct dynamic regions: residues 1–15 likely exchange quickly between multiple conformations on DNA, consistent with a fuzzy complex Fuxreiter, 2018; Tompa and Fuxreiter, 2008; while residues 16–20 (the basic patch) exchange much more slowly and/or between fewer states, leading to signal loss.
evidence: This claim is inferred from NMR linewidth data and is consistent with the concept of fuzzy complexes (Fuxreiter, 2018; Tompa and Fuxreiter, 2008).

claim: The different behavior of H3 and H4 tails may be related to charge distribution and/or positioning relative to the NCP core.
source: This is distinct from the H3 tail, where every residue experiences fast dynamics consistent with a fuzzy complex. The different behavior of the tails may be related to charge distribution and/or positioning relative to the NCP core.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on observed differences in tail dynamics.

claim: The acetylated 15N-H4KS16ac-NCP spectra had additional peaks relative to unmodified NCP, suggesting this modification weakens the H4 tail interaction with DNA.
source: Relative to unmodified NCP, the acetylated NCP spectra had additional peaks (Figure 4d, Figure 4—figure supplement 3), suggesting this modification weakens the H4 tail interaction with DNA (similar to previously observed with the charge neutralization mimetic H4K16Q Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is inferred from NMR data in Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 3, and is consistent with prior studies on H4K16Q (Zhou et al., 2012).

claim: Titration of BPTF BD into the 15N-H4KS16ac-NCP did not lead to any significant CSPs, supporting that H4K16ac was occluded from binding by this reader in the NCP context.
source: Titration of BPTF BD into the 15N-H4KS16ac-NCP did not lead to any significant CSPs, supporting that H4K16ac was occluded from binding by this reader in the NCP context (Figure 4e).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR titration data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: BRD4-BD1 bound H4tetraac peptides with the strongest EC50rel over all peptides tested.
source: BRD4-BD1 has previously been shown to bind acetylated H4 tail peptides Filippakopoulos et al., 2012, and dCypher confirmed the strongest EC50rel for H4tetraac over all peptides tested (Figure 4—figure supplement 3a and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3a and c, and is consistent with Filippakopoulos et al., 2012.

claim: BRD4-BD1 bound H4tetraac in the nucleosome context, though with weaker affinity than the comparable peptide (EC50rel 7.4 nM NCP vs. 0.7 nM peptide).
source: In contrast to BPTF BD, BRD4-BD1 also bound H4tetraac in the nucleosome context, though with weaker affinity than the comparable peptide (EC50rel 7.4 nM NCP vs. 0.7 nM peptide; Figure 4—figure supplement 4b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing peptide and nucleosome binding in Figure 4—figure supplement 4b and c.

claim: Nucleosomal H4 tail accessibility is reader-dependent.
source: Thus, nucleosomal H4 tail accessibility is reader-dependent (also recently demonstrated for PHIP BD1-BD2 Morgan et al., 2021), and the ability to bind may rely on several factors including overall affinity or different engagement mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential binding of BPTF BD vs. BRD4-BD1 to nucleosomal H4, and is consistent with Morgan et al., 2021.

claim: BRD4 BD1 can associate with DNA, and such competition may help disengage the H4 tail from the nucleosome core.
source: For instance, BRD4 BD1 (unlike BPTF BD) can associate with DNA (Miller et al., 2016; Kalra et al., 2022), and such competition may help disengage the H4 tail from the nucleosome core.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on known DNA binding properties of BRD4 BD1 (Miller et al., 2016; Kalra et al., 2022).

claim: To enable binding in the nucleosome context a reader must be able to displace the modified histone tail from DNA.
source: Together, this suggests that to enable binding in the nucleosome context a reader must be able to displace the modified histone tail from DNA.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective data on tail occlusion and reader binding.

claim: Tail accessibility can be enhanced by disrupting the DNA interaction via modification of sidechain charge.
source: Tail accessibility can be enhanced by disrupting the DNA interaction via modification of sidechain charge (Stützer et al., 2016; Morrison et al., 2018), as where distal acetylation of the H3 tail improved BPTF PHD engagement with H3K4me3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b, d and e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b, d, e and citations to prior studies (Stützer et al., 2016; Morrison et al., 2018).

claim: Acetylation does not fully release the tail from DNA binding.
source: Notably, acetylation does not fully release the tail from DNA binding (Morrison et al., 2018; Mutskov et al., 1998), such that the PHD still showed weaker association with the H3K3me3triac NCP relative to peptide.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and citations to prior studies (Morrison et al., 2018; Mutskov et al., 1998).

claim: BPTF BD alone was insufficient to engage the acetylated H3 or H4 tails in the nucleosome context because as a weaker binder it cannot effectively displace even acetylated tails.
source: This may also explain why BPTF BD alone was insufficient to engage the acetylated H3 or H4 tails in the nucleosome context, since as a weaker binder it cannot effectively displace even acetylated tails to engage its reader function.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the binding data showing BD alone cannot bind nucleosomes.

claim: GST-PHD-BD showed 24-fold stronger binding to the cis vs. trans combinatorial context ([H3K4me3K14ac • H3] vs. [H3K4me3 • H3K14ac]).
source: In dCypher assays GST-PHD-BD showed 24-fold stronger binding to the cis vs. trans combinatorial context (EC50rel 10.8 nM [H3K4me3K14ac • H3] vs. 263 nM [H3K4me3 • H3K14ac]; Figure 5a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing cis and trans binding shown in Figure 5a and b.

claim: Binding to the trans combinatorial NCP was indistinguishable from [H3K4me3 • H3], suggesting the tandem reader requires both PTMs in cis.
source: Furthermore, binding to the trans combinatorial NCP was indistinguishable from [H3K4me3 • H3], suggesting the tandem reader requires both PTMs in cis, and trans tail engagement is of minimal contribution.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the binding data showing no enhancement for trans configuration.

claim: GST-PHD-BD had only slightly improved binding to homotypic H3K4me3K14ac over heterotypic [H3K4me3K14ac • H3] (EC50rel 7.3 nM vs. 10.8 nM).
source: Supporting this interaction mechanism, GST-PHD-BD had only slightly improved binding to homotypic H3K4me3K14ac over heterotypic [H3K4me3K14ac • H3] (EC50rel 7.3 nM vs. 10.8 nM; Figure 5a and b), which would be expected if reader engagement to each nucleosomal H3 tail is an essentially independent event.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing homotypic and heterotypic binding in Figure 5a and b.

claim: Reader engagement to each nucleosomal H3 tail is an essentially independent event.
source: Supporting this interaction mechanism, GST-PHD-BD had only slightly improved binding to homotypic H3K4me3K14ac over heterotypic [H3K4me3K14ac • H3] (EC50rel 7.3 nM vs. 10.8 nM; Figure 5a and b), which would be expected if reader engagement to each nucleosomal H3 tail is an essentially independent event.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the small difference in binding between homotypic and heterotypic nucleosomes.

claim: CUT&RUN identified extensive genomic co-localization of BPTF with H3K4me3 and H3K18ac, with the greatest degree of overlap when both are present.
source: To investigate if this preference is recapitulated on chromatin, we performed CUT&RUN with antibodies to BPTF, H3K4me3, and H3K18ac in K562 cells ('Materials and methods' and Supplementary file 2). This identified extensive genomic co-localization of BPTF with each PTM, but the greatest degree of overlap when both are present (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by CUT&RUN data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In reader-CUT&RUN, GST-PHD-BD showed a dramatic preference for spike-in nucleosomes containing H3K4me3triac relative to each PTM alone (sixfold over H3K4me3, 41-fold over H3tetraac).
source: In these controlled studies GST-PHD-BD showed a dramatic preference for spike-ins containing the combinatorial signature (H3K4me3triac) relative to each PTM alone (sixfold over H3K4me3, 41-fold over H3tetraac; Figure 6b), recapitulating our dCypher observations (e.g. Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by reader-CUT&RUN spike-in data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The genomic enrichment of GST-PHD-BD showed extensive overlap with regions containing H3K4me3 and H3K18ac.
source: The genomic enrichment of GST-PHD-BD further confirmed its combinatorial preference, with binding regions showing extensive overlap with those containing H3K4me3 and H3K18ac (Figure 6c and d).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic enrichment data shown in Figure 6c and d.

claim: The genomic enrichment of GST-PHD-BD was highly correlated with that of endogenous BPTF.
source: Furthermore, the genomic enrichment of GST-PHD-BD was also highly correlated with that of endogenous BPTF (Figure 6c and d), supporting that the tandem reader domains are sufficient to drive effective in vivo localization.
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic enrichment data comparing exogenous and endogenous BPTF in Figure 6c and d.

claim: The tandem reader domains are sufficient to drive effective in vivo localization of BPTF.
source: Furthermore, the genomic enrichment of GST-PHD-BD was also highly correlated with that of endogenous BPTF (Figure 6c and d), supporting that the tandem reader domains are sufficient to drive effective in vivo localization.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between exogenous PHD-BD and endogenous BPTF localization.

claim: Nucleosome context strongly influences reader domain engagement with histone PTMs.
source: Taken together, our data indicate that nucleosome context strongly influences reader domain engagement with histone PTMs.
evidence: This is a summary claim synthesizing all the experimental observations in the study.

claim: Multiple reader domains display modified interaction with histone tail PTMs in the nucleosome context.
source: Similarly, multiple reader domains display modified interaction with histone tail PTMs in the nucleosome context (Morrison et al., 2018; Wang and Hayes, 2007; Gatchalian et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2021; Ruthenburg et al., 2011; Spangler et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies documenting context-dependent reader binding.

claim: The default association of nucleosomal histone tails with DNA limits accessibility and requires reader domains to compete for tail engagement.
source: We propose this is due (at least in part) to the default association of nucleosomal histone tails with DNA (Ghoneim et al., 2021), which limits accessibility and requires reader domains to compete for tail engagement.
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on the collective data and is consistent with Ghoneim et al., 2021.

claim: Histone PTMs may play multiple roles: weakening the DNA association to increase access for reader domains, providing a platform for reader domain binding, or both.
source: As a result, histone PTMs may play multiple roles; weakening the DNA association to increase access for reader domains, providing a platform for reader domain binding, or both.
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: A nearly identical conformation of histone tails has been observed in chromatin arrays via solid-state NMR spectroscopy.
source: However, via solid-state NMR spectroscopy, a nearly identical conformation of histone tails has also been observed in chromatin arrays (Musselman and Kutateladze, 2022; Shi et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2013; Xiang et al., 2018), and the H3 tail: DNA interaction has been observed in vivo by ChIP-exo (Rhee et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to solid-state NMR studies on chromatin arrays (Musselman and Kutateladze, 2022; Shi et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2013; Xiang et al., 2018) and in vivo ChIP-exo (Rhee et al., 2014).

claim: The H3 tail:DNA interaction has been observed in vivo by ChIP-exo.
source: However, via solid-state NMR spectroscopy, a nearly identical conformation of histone tails has also been observed in chromatin arrays (Musselman and Kutateladze, 2022; Shi et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2013; Xiang et al., 2018), and the H3 tail: DNA interaction has been observed in vivo by ChIP-exo (Rhee et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rhee et al., 2014.

claim: H3K4me3 is invariably seen in (and most effectively created in) the cis context of H3 tail acetylation.
source: We also note that H3K4me3 is invariably seen in (and most effectively created in) the cis context of H3 tail acetylation (see below) (Jain et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jain et al., 2023.

claim: The preference of BPTF PHD-BD for H3K4me3 with H3K14ac or H3K18ac over H3K9ac may be due to the in cis proximity of K9 to H3K4me3, restricting BD binding when the PHD finger is engaged.
source: The preference of BPTF PHD-BD for H3K4me3 with H3K14ac or H3K18ac over H3K9ac may be due to the in cis proximity of K9 to H3K4me3, restricting BD binding when the PHD finger is engaged.
evidence: This is a mechanistic speculation based on structural considerations.

claim: H3 acetylation-mediated switch increases tail accessibility in the nucleosome context and improves MLL1C-mediated H3K4 methylation.
source: Our observations on co-incident tail acetylation promoting H3K4 accessibility to BPTF PHD reader (this study) are also exhibited by MLL1C methyltransferase (Jain et al., 2023). There we identified a H3 acetylation-mediated switch that increases tail accessibility in the nucleosome context, and thus improves MLL1C-mediated H3K4 methylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jain et al., 2023.

claim: H3 acetylation enhances MLL1C activity in cis but has no impact in trans.
source: Evidence for this model includes an increased Kcat (enhanced tail accessibility leads to an increase in substrate concentration), and that H3 acetylation enhances MLL1C activity in cis but has no impact in trans (demonstrated with heterotypic nucleosomes).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to data from Jain et al., 2023.

claim: Middle-down MS on bulk chromatin shows that H3 tail acetylation invariably accompanies cis H3K4 methylation.
source: Furthermore, middle-down MS on bulk chromatin shows that H3 tail acetylation invariably accompanies cis H3K4 methylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to mass spectrometry data, likely from Jain et al., 2023.

claim: Individual reader domains consistently show reduced affinity and restricted specificity when moving from peptide to nucleosome context.
source: When moving from the peptide to nucleosome context we (and others) consistently observe individual reader domains to show reduced affinity and restricted specificity (Jain et al., 2023; Morrison et al., 2018; Wang and Hayes, 2007; Gatchalian et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2021; Marunde et al., 2022a; Morgan et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from this study and multiple citations to prior work.

claim: PWWP readers form multivalent interactions with DNA and histone tails, so peptide studies are often uninformative.
source: An exception to this is readers with intrinsic DNA binding ability, such as the PWWPs. These form multivalent interactions with DNA and histone tails (so peptide studies are often uninformative) (Eidahl et al., 2013; van Nuland et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2020; Dukatz et al., 2019; Tian et al., 2019; Weinberg et al., 2019; Dilworth et al., 2022), but may also act to directly compete for the DNA, thus promoting tail accessibility when the target engaged (Weaver et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations documenting PWWP reader behavior (Eidahl et al., 2013; van Nuland et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2020; Dukatz et al., 2019; Tian et al., 2019; Weinberg et al., 2019; Dilworth et al., 2022; Weaver et al., 2018).

claim: Modification of an adjacent tail may alter the dynamics of the target tail, such trans-tail crosstalk being recently reported for H3 and H4.
source: Beyond in cis modification of the target histone tail (as in this study), modification of an adjacent tail may alter the dynamics of the target, such trans-tail crosstalk being recently reported for H3 and H4 (Furukawa et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Furukawa et al., 2020.

claim: Histone tail accessibility can be modulated by changes to the canonical nucleosome composition, such as hexasomes depleted of one H2A-H2B dimer.
source: Alternatively, histone tail accessibility can be modulated by changes to the canonical nucleosome composition, such as hexasomes depleted of one H2A-H2B dimer (Morrison et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Morrison et al., 2021.

claim: In reader-CUT&RUN, GST-PHD-BD recapitulated the dCypher preference for spike-in nucleosomes containing the combinatorial target (H3K4me3triac) over each PTM class alone.
source: In reader-CUT&RUN GST-PHD-BD recapitulated the dCypher preference for spike-in Nucs containing the combinatorial target (H3K4me3triac) over each PTM class alone (Figure 6b).
evidence: This claim is supported by reader-CUT&RUN data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The combinatorial readout of H3K4me3 and H3K18ac is a discerning factor in the genomic localization of BPTF.
source: Together, this suggests that the combinatorial readout of these PTMs is indeed a discerning factor in the genomic localization of BPTF: the activity of both domains is clearly important to achieve robust interaction, and thus at minimum critical to achieve proper kinetics on chromatin.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the genomic localization data showing correlation between PTMs and BPTF binding.

claim: There are increasing examples of auto-regulatory elements within CAPs that modulate their activity.
source: Indeed, there are increasing examples of auto-regulatory elements within CAPs that modulate their activity (Guo et al., 2015; Ruan et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2015; Misaki et al., 2016; Andrews et al., 2016b; Harrison et al., 2016; Ludwigsen et al., 2017; Isaac et al., 2017; Slaughter et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019; Tencer et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2021; Nodelman et al., 2021; Weinberg et al., 2021), suggesting that a histone code is more than the simple availability of potentially redundant positive signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by numerous citations documenting auto-regulatory mechanisms in chromatin-associated proteins.

claim: The 'histone code' is ultimately defined by a combination of three elements: (1) the PTMs that can be recognized and bound by individual reader domains; (2) accessibility of the modified histone tails in the nucleosome context; and (3) the organization and multivalent binding potential of grouped domains.
source: We propose the 'histone code' is ultimately defined by a combination of three elements: (1) the PTMs that can be recognized and bound by individual reader domains; (2) accessibility of the modified histone tails in the nucleosome context; and (3) the organization and multivalent binding potential of grouped domains (where the whole is greater than the sum of the parts).
evidence: This is a conceptual framework proposed based on all the experimental observations in the study.
